Bonded composite patches provide a structurally efficient alternative load path that can repair live fatigue cracks, unlike mechanically fastened metallic patches which require crack removal or termination.
Boron/epoxy (b/ep) composites have a Young's modulus about three times that of aluminum and are chosen for their mechanical properties and low electrical conductivity.
Patch thickness is minimized due to the high stiffness of composites, with typical patch curing temperatures between 80°C and 120°C.
Fatigue failure modes include transverse fatigue of composite fibers and disbonding at adhesive or interface layers.
The patch system is divided into a safe-life zone at tapered ends with low allowable strain and a damage-tolerant zone in the middle where slow disbond growth is acceptable.
Disbond growth rate correlates with adhesive shear strain range, with a threshold below which disbond initiation is unlikely.
Generic bonded joint tests, such as double-overlap joints, are used to establish fatigue allowables for patch design.
Analytical crack growth models incorporating thermal residual stresses predict patched crack growth rates accurately under spectrum loading.
Environmental durability is a critical concern due to moisture sensitivity of metal-adhesive interfaces, which can cause catastrophic bond failure.
The Boeing wedge test (BWT) is used to assess bond durability and surface preparation quality before patch application.
Non-destructive inspection methods currently cannot reliably detect weak or degrading bonds unless disbonding is obvious.
Thermal residual stresses from coefficient of thermal expansion mismatch induce tensile mean stresses affecting fatigue crack growth.
The Fail-Safe approach requires the repaired structure to withstand design limit loads even if the patch fails, necessitating inspection based on unpatched crack growth.
Smart patch systems monitor their own health to detect damage or loss of patch integrity, enabling immediate detection.
Australian F111 aircraft repairs using bonded composite patches have successfully prevented crack growth for multiple years in service.
Adhesive bonding is sensitive to surface contamination, requiring strict quality control and technician qualification.
Patch system fatigue efficiency includes recovery of residual strength and reduction in crack growth rate.
Design of tapered patch ends and adhesive thickness control strain levels to prevent fatigue damage initiation.
Fatigue crack growth under bonded patches can be predicted using modified crack closure models.
Environmental degradation can reduce the disbonding threshold to zero, making inspection intervals ineffective without durability assurance.
